description: Somos estudiantes de 5to año del Colegio San Cayetano apasionados por la tecnología, la programación y la IA. Nuestro interés es resolver problemas rurales reales. ¿Por qué unirte? Porque aquí transformamos el código en un impacto social real, creando herramientas sustentables que protegen nuestras huertas. ¡Buscamos mentes creativas dispuestas a innovar y sumar su talento!
summary:
We developed AgroScan: Ecological Guardians to help families in Pozuelos and Vinará, Santiago del Estero, Argentina, decide what to plant, how to conserve water, and which part of their plot to check first. We are fifth-year secondary school students and teachers at Colegio San Cayetano. Using tablets from the Metas Digitales program, we built a free app that families can set up online at the Pozuelos municipal center and use offline in the field.

For the Field Shift challenge, AgroScan helps families compare three crop rotation strategies based on soil moisture, NASA POWER climate data, and their own priorities. Families can compare observations from drone flights over the same plot, explore how the crop might change, and record a task to check that prediction on the ground. The app also helps families interpret drinking water laboratory reports and identify which tests are missing.

In a community where many families must leave home for seasonal work, we want the technology we learn at school to give us more opportunities to care for our crops, share what we learn, and choose to live and work in our hometown.
details:
We developed AgroScan · Ecological Guardians to help farming families in Pozuelos and Vinará, in the Río Hondo Department of Santiago del Estero, Argentina, decide what to plant, how to conserve water, and which part of their plot to inspect first. We are fifth-year secondary school students and their teachers at Instituto San Cayetano LL45. We designed the app for people who work alone, have limited connectivity, and sometimes need to leave their crops unattended to accompany a family member to the hospital in Termas de Río Hondo.

How it works. The Field Shift simulator combines climate data from NASA POWER with surface soil moisture scenarios based on NASA’s SMAP mission. For a plot that previously grew tomatoes, farmers can compare three options: plant tomatoes or potatoes next season, rotate with legumes such as cowpeas or vetch, or grow butternut squash and corn together to sell at local markets. Farmers choose what matters most to them—saving water, earning income, or managing the plot with little help—and compare the benefits, risks, and field checks for each option. For example, they can see what happens when simulated soil moisture drops to 14%. Using 18% as a reference threshold in the demo, AgroScan suggests keeping crop residue on the soil surface and checking moisture in the field before planting.

From observation to action. The Community Patrol module lets families compare drone observations of the same area on different dates. In our simulated strawberry plot, visible crop cover falls from 62% to 58% and then to 54%. That decline raises a question the family can investigate: Are the drip emitters watering the plot evenly? A family member can save a 15-minute task in the Vigía alert module, share it with a neighbor, and record what they find. The Leaf Lab lets them add a leaf photo to the field record. For water from a well, a cistern, collected rainfall, or an aboveground farm tank, the app distinguishes between irrigation and drinking water. For drinking water, it helps families read a laboratory report, identify missing tests, and compare results from a follow-up sample after a professional has recommended corrective action.

Tools and design choices. We built a progressive web app using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. A service worker makes the app available offline, and the Rural Notebook stores observations on the device. Families can update the app and its data at the Pozuelos municipal center, take the tablet to their plot, and record observations without a signal. We designed the interface for mobile phones and the school tablets provided through the Metas Digitales program. We label simulated examples and distinguish between what a satellite can show at a regional scale, what a drone can reveal within a plot, and what someone can verify only by walking the crop rows.

Creativity and expected impact. Our contribution is to connect those three perspectives to a decision a family can make that day and check afterward. We hope AgroScan will help families decide where to inspect first, conserve irrigation water, and keep a useful history of each plot. For our school, the project is also about being able to put down roots. In an area where many people must leave home for seasonal work, we want learning to code and studying Earth science to give us more opportunities to live and work in our own community.
